concepts.name: Founding and Organizational Structure of Arya Samaj
key_dimensions: Founded in Bombay (1875), later headquartered in Lahore — UPSC trap: often confused with founding city vs. operational base
Ten Principles (Niyamas) of Arya Samaj and their socio-religious implications
Distinction between Arya Samaj as a reform body vs. a revivalist body — the 'Back to the Vedas' paradox
Comparison with Brahmo Samaj in terms of organizational structure and geographic spread

concepts.name: Dayanand Saraswati's Intellectual and Theological Framework
key_dimensions: Rejection of idol worship, polytheism, and Puranic Hinduism — basis in Vedic monotheism
Satyarth Prakash (1875) as the foundational text — its content, editions, and controversies
Influence of Swami Virajanand on Dayanand's ideological transformation
Dayanand's concept of 'one God, one book' — contrast with other reform movements that accepted plurality

concepts.name: Satyarth Prakash: Content, Significance, and Controversies
key_dimensions: Structure: critique of other religions (Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Jainism) alongside Hindu reform — UPSC trap: its adversarial tone vs. syncretic reformers
Role in shaping Hindu nationalist consciousness and its double-edged legacy
Language choice (Hindi/Braj Bhasha) and its significance for vernacular intellectual culture
Comparison with Brahmo texts like 'Brahmo Dharma' in terms of theological exclusivity vs. inclusivity

concepts.name: Shuddhi Movement: Reconversion and Its Political Implications
key_dimensions: Origins, purpose, and mechanism of the Shuddhi ritual for reconverting Christians and Muslims
Distinction between Dayanand's original Shuddhi and its later aggressive use by Arya Samaj leaders (e.g., Swami Shraddhanand)
Role of Shuddhi in shaping Hindu-Muslim communal tensions in early 20th century Punjab
UPSC trap: Shuddhi vs. Sangathan — understanding both as Arya Samaj-linked responses to perceived Hindu demographic threat

concepts.name: Dayanand's Vedic Authoritarianism vs. Rationalism — The Ideological Tension
key_dimensions: Dayanand's rejection of superstition and caste hierarchy as rational, yet his insistence on Vedic infallibility as the sole authority
How this differs from Brahmo Samaj's reason-based theology (Ram Mohan Roy) and Ramakrishna's experiential mysticism
UPSC trap: Dayanand is often labeled a 'rationalist' but his Vedic literalism places him differently from Western rationalists
His opposition to child marriage, widow remarriage support — reform credentials within a conservative textual framework

concepts.name: Arya Samaj and the Caste Question
key_dimensions: Dayanand's rejection of hereditary caste (Jati) in favor of Varna based on merit/Guna-Karma — a nuanced position often tested
UPSC trap: Dayanand did NOT abolish varna; he redefined it — contrast with Phule and Ambedkar who rejected varna entirely
Dayanand Anglophone Colleges (DAV) and their role in Dalit upliftment — practical vs. theoretical positions
Comparison with Brahmo Samaj and Prarthana Samaj on caste reform radicalism

concepts.name: DAV Schools and Colleges: Education as Reform Strategy
key_dimensions: DAV (Dayanand Anglo-Vedic) institutions — founded after Dayanand's death, 1886, Lahore — UPSC trap: Dayanand himself did not establish DAV
Gurukul vs. DAV split within Arya Samaj: Lala Hansraj (DAV/Western) vs. Munshi Ram/Swami Shraddhanand (Gurukul/traditional)
Role of Lala Lajpat Rai in DAV movement and the political nexus between Arya Samaj and early nationalism
Significance of Gurukul Kangri (1902) as an experiment in indigenizing education

concepts.name: Arya Samaj's Role in Fostering Indian Nationalism
key_dimensions: Link between Arya Samaj ideology and early nationalist leaders: Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal (tangentially), Swami Shraddhanand
Concept of 'Aryan pride' and its role in constructing a Hindu nationalist identity pre-dating the RSS
UPSC trap: Arya Samaj is associated with nationalism but remained socially reformist — not the same as Hindu Mahasabha or RSS ideology
Punjab as the epicenter: Why Arya Samaj flourished in Punjab and its role in countering Christian missionary activity

concepts.name: Arya Samaj vs. Brahmo Samaj: A Comparative Framework
key_dimensions: Theological base: Vedic monotheism (Arya) vs. Universal theism/reason (Brahmo)
Attitude to Western influence: Arya Samaj's indigenism vs. Brahmo Samaj's liberal Westernism
Geographic and social base: Punjab/North India (Arya) vs. Bengal/urban elite (Brahmo)
UPSC trap: Both opposed idol worship and caste rigidity but for different reasons and to different extents

concepts.name: Arya Samaj vs. Ramakrishna Mission: Reform vs. Revival Debate
key_dimensions: Ramakrishna's acceptance of image worship vs. Dayanand's absolute rejection — doctrinal fault line
Vivekananda's universalism vs. Dayanand's Vedic exclusivism
Both movements contributed to Hindu self-assertion but through opposing methodologies
UPSC trap: Both are sometimes grouped as 'revivalist' — but Ramakrishna Mission had a universalist and service-oriented dimension absent in early Arya Samaj

concepts.name: Dayanand's Position on Women's Rights and Social Reforms
key_dimensions: Support for women's education and widow remarriage — progressive credentials
Opposition to child marriage and purdah system
UPSC trap: Dayanand supported women's Vedic education but within a patriarchal Vedic framework — not feminist in the modern sense
Comparison with Ram Mohan Roy (Sati abolition), Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (widow remarriage) on women's reform — who went further?

concepts.name: Sangathan Movement and Arya Samaj's Response to Communalism
key_dimensions: Sangathan as a Hindu consolidation movement — closely linked to Arya Samaj in post-1920s Punjab
Swami Shraddhanand's role and his assassination (1926) — impact on Hindu-Muslim relations
UPSC trap: Sangathan and Shuddhi together created a cycle of communal mobilization (Tabligh and Tanzim as Muslim responses)
Gandhi's response to Shraddhanand's murder and the Congress-Arya Samaj relationship

concepts.name: Dayanand's Critique of Christianity and Islam
key_dimensions: Satyarth Prakash's chapters explicitly critiquing Biblical and Quranic authority — unique among 19th-century reformers
UPSC trap: This adversarial approach sets Dayanand apart from syncretic reformers like Kabir or Ram Mohan Roy who found common ground
Impact of this critique on communal identity formation in colonial Punjab
Contrast with Vivekananda's Parliament of Religions approach (acceptance of religious plurality)

concepts.name: Arya Samaj and the Hindi-Urdu-Sanskrit Language Controversy
key_dimensions: Dayanand's promotion of Hindi in Devanagari script as a nationalist and reform tool
Arya Samaj's role in the Hindi movement in Punjab and Hindi-Urdu controversy
UPSC trap: Language politics of Arya Samaj often overlaps with Hindu nationalist politics — important to separate reform from identity politics
Contrast with Aligarh Movement's promotion of Urdu as a Muslim identity marker

concepts.name: Dayanand's Death and the Conspiracy Question
key_dimensions: Circumstances of death (1883, Ajmer) — alleged poisoning by a courtesan, Nanhi Jan, reportedly at instigation of Maharaja of Jodhpur
UPSC relevance: This episode reflects the political resistance of princely states to reform movements
How Dayanand's death accelerated institutionalization of Arya Samaj
Comparison with other reformers who faced elite resistance (Jyotiba Phule, Basavanna)

concepts.name: Arya Samaj's Role in Dalit Upliftment: Promises and Limitations
key_dimensions: Arya Samaj ran schools for lower castes and used Shuddhi to 'reclaim' Dalits — but within a Hindu fold strategy
UPSC trap: Arya Samaj's Dalit work was driven partly by demographic anxieties about conversion, not purely emancipatory
Contrast with Jyotiba Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj which fundamentally rejected Brahminical authority that Arya Samaj retained
Ambedkar's critique of Arya Samaj — accepting Vedic authority meant accepting the source of caste oppression

concepts.name: Concept of 'Back to the Vedas' — Reformist or Revivalist?
key_dimensions: UPSC trap: Arya Samaj is simultaneously classified as 'reformist' (social changes) and 'revivalist' (return to Vedic authority) — understanding the dual nature is critical
How 'Back to the Vedas' was a selective reading — Dayanand used Vedas to delegitimize practices like idol worship, caste by birth
Comparison with Islamic reformism (Wahhabism/'Back to Quran') — structural parallel tested in mains
Historians' debate: Bipan Chandra's view of Arya Samaj as reform movement vs. critics who see it as Hindu revivalism

concepts.name: Arya Samaj in Punjab: Socio-Political Context and Impact
key_dimensions: Punjab's unique demographic (Hindu-Muslim-Sikh) and colonial context explaining Arya Samaj's rapid growth there
Competition with Singh Sabha (Sikh reform) and their overlapping yet distinct identities — UPSC trap: both reform Punjabi traditions but diverge sharply on Vedic authority
Arya Samaj's role in the census-driven communal headcount anxiety under British India
Impact on emergence of Hindu communal politics in Punjab leading up to Partition

concepts.name: Lala Lajpat Rai and the Political Legacy of Arya Samaj
key_dimensions: Lajpat Rai as the bridge between Arya Samaj ideology and Bal-Pal-Lal extremist nationalism
UPSC trap: Lajpat Rai was influenced by Arya Samaj but his politics were not theocratic — he was a modern nationalist
His writings (Unhappy India, Young India) and their connection to Arya Samaj's anti-colonial self-assertion
Comparison with Tilak (Hinduism as political tool) and Gandhi (religion as moral force) in using religious identity for nationalism

concepts.name: Gurukul System vs. Western Education: The Internal Arya Samaj Debate
key_dimensions: Post-1886 split: DAV faction (Lala Hansraj) accepting English/Western curriculum vs. Gurukul faction (Swami Shraddhanand) insisting on indigenous Vedic education
Gurukul Kangri at Haridwar (1902) — curriculum, residential system, and its neo-traditionalist vision
UPSC trap: Both factions belonged to Arya Samaj — this internal conflict shows reformist movements are not monolithic
Parallels with broader colonial-era debate between Macaulay's Anglicism and Orientalism — how Arya Samaj navigated it internally
